claim: Dedifferentiation of acini to duct-like cells occurs during the physiologic damage response in the pancreas.
source: Dedifferentiation of acini to duct-like cells occurs during the physiologic damage response in the pancreas, but this process can be co-opted by oncogenic Kras to drive carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about a known biological process in the pancreas, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Dedifferentiation of acini to duct-like cells can be co-opted by oncogenic Kras to drive carcinogenesis.
source: Dedifferentiation of acini to duct-like cells occurs during the physiologic damage response in the pancreas, but this process can be co-opted by oncogenic Kras to drive carcinogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript and references to prior knowledge.

claim: Myeloid cells infiltrate the pancreas during the onset of pancreatic cancer.
source: Myeloid cells infiltrate the pancreas during the onset of pancreatic cancer, and promote carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing myeloid cell presence in the pancreas during early carcinogenesis.

claim: Myeloid cells promote carcinogenesis during the onset of pancreatic cancer.
source: Myeloid cells infiltrate the pancreas during the onset of pancreatic cancer, and promote carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from myeloid cell depletion studies showing reduced PanIN formation.

claim: The function of infiltrating myeloid cells is regulated by oncogenic Kras expressed in epithelial cells.
source: Here, we show that the function of infiltrating myeloid cells is regulated by oncogenic Kras expressed in epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing changes in myeloid cell behavior upon Kras activation/inactivation.

claim: In the presence of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote acinar dedifferentiation and carcinogenesis.
source: In the presence of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote acinar dedifferentiation and carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that myeloid cell depletion in the presence of oncogenic Kras leads to acinar redifferentiation.

claim: Upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote re-differentiation of acinar cells.
source: Upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote re-differentiation of acinar cells, remodeling of the fibrotic stroma and tissue repair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing impaired acinar redifferentiation when myeloid cells are depleted after Kras inactivation.

claim: Upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote remodeling of the fibrotic stroma.
source: Upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote re-differentiation of acinar cells, remodeling of the fibrotic stroma and tissue repair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing persistent fibrosis when myeloid cells are depleted after Kras inactivation.

claim: Upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote tissue repair.
source: Upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells promote re-differentiation of acinar cells, remodeling of the fibrotic stroma and tissue repair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing impaired tissue repair when myeloid cells are depleted after Kras inactivation.

claim: Both aspects of myeloid cell activity depend, at least in part, on activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling.
source: Intriguingly, both aspects of myeloid cell activity depend, at least in part, on activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling, with different subsets of ligands and receptors in different target cells promoting carcinogenesis or repair, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in EGFR ligand expression and MAPK activation in different cellular compartments.

claim: Different subsets of EGFR ligands and receptors in different target cells promote carcinogenesis or repair.
source: Intriguingly, both aspects of myeloid cell activity depend, at least in part, on activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling, with different subsets of ligands and receptors in different target cells promoting carcinogenesis or repair, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential expression of EGFR ligands (HB-EGF, EGF, TGFα) and receptors (EGFR, ERBB4) during carcinogenesis versus repair.

claim: The cross-talk between epithelial cells and infiltrating myeloid cells determines the balance between tissue repair and carcinogenesis in the pancreas.
source: Thus, the cross-talk between epithelial cells and infiltrating myeloid cells determines the balance between tissue repair and carcinogenesis in the pancreas.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data showing bidirectional regulation between epithelial and myeloid cells.

claim: The highly specialized epithelial cells in the adult pancreas derive from common progenitors during embryogenesis.
source: The highly specialized epithelial cells in the adult pancreas (Slack, 1995) derive from common progenitors during embryogenesis (Cano et al., 2007; Gittes, 2009; Means and Leach, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acinar, ductal and centroacinar cells constitute the likely origin of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
source: The cells forming the exocrine pancreas, namely acinar, ductal and centroacinar cells, are believed to constitute the likely origin of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer and one of the deadliest human malignancies (for review, see (Puri and Hebrok, 2010; Rooman and Real, 2012; Stanger and Dor, 2006; Zorn and Wells, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common type of pancreatic cancer.
source: The cells forming the exocrine pancreas, namely acinar, ductal and centroacinar cells, are believed to constitute the likely origin of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer and one of the deadliest human malignancies (for review, see (Puri and Hebrok, 2010; Rooman and Real, 2012; Stanger and Dor, 2006; Zorn and Wells, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is one of the deadliest human malignancies.
source: The cells forming the exocrine pancreas, namely acinar, ductal and centroacinar cells, are believed to constitute the likely origin of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer and one of the deadliest human malignancies (for review, see (Puri and Hebrok, 2010; Rooman and Real, 2012; Stanger and Dor, 2006; Zorn and Wells, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Kras mutations are common in human pancreatic cancer.
source: Kras mutations are common in human pancreatic cancer (Bailey et al., 2016; Hezel et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2008), and are present with high frequency in the precursor lesions to pancreatic cancer known as Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN) (Kanda et al., 2012; Klimstra and Longnecker, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Kras mutations are present with high frequency in Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN).
source: Kras mutations are common in human pancreatic cancer (Bailey et al., 2016; Hezel et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2008), and are present with high frequency in the precursor lesions to pancreatic cancer known as Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN) (Kanda et al., 2012; Klimstra and Longnecker, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetically engineered mice that express oncogenic Kras in the pancreas develop PanINs that progress to pancreatic cancer.
source: Genetically engineered mice that express oncogenic Kras in the pancreas develop PanINs that progress to pancreatic cancer (Aguirre et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2005), a process that is accelerated by the introduction of other common mutations, such as mutation or loss of tumor suppressors p53 and Ink4a/ARF (Aguirre et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PanIN progression to pancreatic cancer is accelerated by the introduction of mutations in tumor suppressors p53 and Ink4a/ARF.
source: Genetically engineered mice that express oncogenic Kras in the pancreas develop PanINs that progress to pancreatic cancer (Aguirre et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2005), a process that is accelerated by the introduction of other common mutations, such as mutation or loss of tumor suppressors p53 and Ink4a/ARF (Aguirre et al., 2003; Hingorani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mice, both ductal and acinar cells can serve as the cell of origin for pancreatic cancer.
source: In mice, both ductal and acinar cells can serve as the cell of origin for pancreatic cancer (De La O et al., 2008; Guerra et al., 2007; Habbe et al., 2008; von Figura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acini are more susceptible to transformation than ductal cells, through a process of dedifferentiation known as acinar-ductal metaplasia (ADM).
source: However, acini are more susceptible to transformation, through a process of dedifferentiation known as acinar-ductal metaplasia (ADM) (Kopp et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: ADM is a reversible physiological process that protects the pancreas upon tissue injury, such as acute pancreatitis.
source: ADM is a reversible physiological process that protects the pancreas upon tissue injury, such as acute pancreatitis (Halbrook et al., 2017; Houbracken et al., 2011; Strobel et al., 2007) in part by reducing the production of digestive enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADM protects the pancreas in part by reducing the production of digestive enzymes.
source: ADM is a reversible physiological process that protects the pancreas upon tissue injury, such as acute pancreatitis (Halbrook et al., 2017; Houbracken et al., 2011; Strobel et al., 2007) in part by reducing the production of digestive enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and established knowledge.

claim: In presence of oncogenic Kras, pancreatitis-induced ADM becomes irreversible and progresses to PanIN lesions.
source: In presence of oncogenic Kras, pancreatitis-induced ADM becomes irreversible and progresses to PanIN lesions (Carrière et al., 2009; Guerra et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The iKras* mouse model allows inducible and reversible expression of oncogenic Kras upon administration of doxycycline (DOX).
source: We have previously described the iKras* mouse model, which allows inducible and reversible expression of oncogenic Kras upon administration of doxycycline (DOX) (Collins et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Sustained Kras activity is necessary to maintain ADM as well as PanIN lesions.
source: By inactivating oncogenic Kras at different stages of carcinogenesis, we showed that sustained Kras activity is necessary to maintain ADM as well as PanIN lesions, and inactivation of oncogenic Kras leads to redifferentiation of acinar cells (Collins et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras leads to redifferentiation of acinar cells.
source: By inactivating oncogenic Kras at different stages of carcinogenesis, we showed that sustained Kras activity is necessary to maintain ADM as well as PanIN lesions, and inactivation of oncogenic Kras leads to redifferentiation of acinar cells (Collins et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Kras-driven de-differentiation of the acinar cell compartment is mediated, at least in part, by activation of the Kras effector pathway MAPK/ERK.
source: Kras-driven de-differentiation of the acinar cell compartment is mediated, at least in part, by activation of the Kras effector pathway MAPK/ERK (Collins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The acinar cell specific transcription factors PTF1A and BHLHA15, as well as the pancreatic transcription factor PDX1, protect cellular identity and thus counteract transformation.
source: Conversely, the acinar cell specific transcription factors PTF1A and BHLHA15, as well as the pancreatic transcription factor PDX1, protect cellular identity and thus counteract transformation (Krah et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophages and other myeloid subsets are required for PanIN formation.
source: Macrophages and other myeloid subsets are required for PanIN formation (Liou et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017) and might be sufficient to induce ADM (Liou et al., 2015; Liou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophages might be sufficient to induce ADM.
source: Macrophages and other myeloid subsets are required for PanIN formation (Liou et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017) and might be sufficient to induce ADM (Liou et al., 2015; Liou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies, but stated as a possibility.

claim: Macrophages are important for pancreas regeneration following acute damage, such as experimental loss of acinar cells.
source: Macrophages are similarly important for pancreas regeneration following acute damage, such as experimental loss of acinar cells (Criscimanna et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DT injection resulted in a 40–45% decrease of pancreas infiltrating CD11b+ cells.
source: Compared to control, DT injection resulted in a 40–45% decrease of pancreas infiltrating CD11b+ cells; we observed similar depletion of macrophages and Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), but little change in the dendritic cell population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DT treatment resulted in similar depletion of macrophages and Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), but little change in the dendritic cell population.
source: Compared to control, DT injection resulted in a 40–45% decrease of pancreas infiltrating CD11b+ cells; we observed similar depletion of macrophages and Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), but little change in the dendritic cell population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: One week following myeloid depletion, occasional acini, increased ADM and fewer mucinous lesions and PanINs were observed compared to control iKras* tissues.
source: In contrast, 1 week following myeloid depletion, we observed occasional acini, increased ADM and fewer mucinous lesions and PanINs than in corresponding iKras* tissues (Figure 1C, quantification in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion resulted in a reduction in MAPK activation in epithelial cells notwithstanding the continuous presence of oncogenic Kras.
source: Furthermore, upon myeloid cell depletion, we observed a reduction in MAPK activation in epithelial cells (as determined by p-ERK1/2 immunostaining) notwithstanding the continuous presence of oncogenic Kras (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The reduction in MAPK signaling correlated with an increase of acinar differentiation in the tissue.
source: This reduction in MAPK signaling correlated with an increase of acinar differentiation in the tissue, as determined by staining for Basic helix-loop-helix family member a15 (BHLHA15, also known as MIST1) (Figure 1F) and for Amylase, a digestive enzyme (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Co-expression of acinar markers (BHLHA15 and Amylase) with the ductal marker CK19 was observed, possibly indicating ongoing re-differentiation of acinar cells.
source: We also observed co-expression of acinar markers (BHLHA15 and Amylase) with the ductal marker CK19, possibly indicating ongoing re-differentiation of acinar cells (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G, with interpretation as speculation.

claim: Both PanIN/ADM lesions and recovered acinar cells expressed EGFP, validating the redifferentiation of acini from low-grade lesions.
source: Our results showed that both PanIN/ADM lesions and recovered acinar cells expressed EGFP, thus validating the redifferentiation of acini from low-grade lesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion resulted in a reduction in intracellular mucin, as measured by Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) staining.
source: We also observed a reduction in intracellular mucin, as measured by Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) staining (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No changes in apoptosis were observed following myeloid cell depletion in the presence of oncogenic Kras.
source: We did not observe changes in apoptosis (Cleaved Caspase three staining, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion led to reduced expression of Smooth Muscle Actin (SMA), a fibroblast activation marker.
source: Although tissue fibrosis was still evident by histology (Figure 1C), we observed reduced expression of Smooth Muscle Actin (SMA), a fibroblast activation marker (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: The expression of genes for the production of extracellular matrix components, such as Fibronectin 1 (Fn1), Collagen type I alpha one chain (Col1a1) and Collagen type III alpha one chain (Col3a1), was reduced upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: Consistently, the expression of genes for the production of extracellular matrix components, such as Fibronectin 1 (Fn1), Collagen type I alpha one chain (Col1a1) and Collagen type III alpha one chain (Col3a1), was reduced (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (Shh), secreted by pancreatic neoplastic cells to activate surrounding fibroblasts, was reduced upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: Sonic hedgehog (Shh), secreted by pancreatic neoplastic cells to activate surrounding fibroblasts (Bailey et al., 2008; Yauch et al., 2008), was similarly reduced upon myeloid cell depletion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Ligand-mediated activation of EGFR is required to maintain elevated Kras/MAPK activity even in presence of oncogenic Kras.
source: Even in presence of oncogenic Kras, ligand-mediated activation of EGFR is required to maintain elevated Kras/MAPK activity (Ardito et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of the EGFR ligand Heparin-Binding epidermal-growth-factor (EGF)-like growth factor (Hbegf) decreased upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the EGFR ligand Heparin-Binding epidermal-growth-factor (EGF)-like growth factor (Hbegf) −previously shown to promote pancreatic carcinogenesis (Ardito et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014)− decreased upon myeloid cell depletion, suggesting that myeloid cells might be a source of this factor or regulate its expression in other compartments (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Hbegf has been previously shown to promote pancreatic carcinogenesis.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the EGFR ligand Heparin-Binding epidermal-growth-factor (EGF)-like growth factor (Hbegf) −previously shown to promote pancreatic carcinogenesis (Ardito et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014)− decreased upon myeloid cell depletion, suggesting that myeloid cells might be a source of this factor or regulate its expression in other compartments (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myeloid cells might be a source of Hbegf or regulate its expression in other compartments.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the EGFR ligand Heparin-Binding epidermal-growth-factor (EGF)-like growth factor (Hbegf) −previously shown to promote pancreatic carcinogenesis (Ardito et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014)− decreased upon myeloid cell depletion, suggesting that myeloid cells might be a source of this factor or regulate its expression in other compartments (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Hbegf expression decreases upon myeloid cell depletion.

claim: The expression of Epiregulin (Ereg) decreased upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: We observed a similar pattern for Epiregulin (Ereg), which decreased upon myeloid cell depletion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: There was no change in three other EGFR ligand genes, Amphiregulin (Areg), Transforming growth factor α (Tgfα) and Egf, upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: In contrast, there was no change in three other EGFR ligand genes, Amphiregulin (Areg), Transforming growth factor α (Tgfα) and Egf.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: p-EGFR was expressed in epithelial cells in the control as well as up to three days following myeloid cell depletion, but virtually complete loss of expression by one week.
source: Immunostaining for the active, phosphorylated form of EGFR (p-EGFR), showed expression in in epithelial cells in the control as well as up to three days following myeloid cell depletion, but virtually complete loss of expression by one week (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Myeloid cells – either directly or through interaction with other cell types – are required for activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in epithelial cells, thus promoting carcinogenesis while preventing acinar re-differentiation and tissue repair.
source: Our data support the notion that myeloid cells – either directly or through interaction with other cell types – are required for activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in epithelial cells, thus promoting carcinogenesis while preventing acinar re-differentiation and tissue repair.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In advanced malignancy, myeloid cells promote tumorigenesis by inhibiting CD8+ T cell mediated immune responses.
source: In advanced malignancy, myeloid cells promote tumorigenesis by inhibiting CD8+ T cell mediated immune responses (Mitchem et al., 2013; Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2014), and myeloid cell depletion causes CD8+ T cell mediated epithelial cell death.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion causes CD8+ T cell mediated epithelial cell death in advanced malignancy.
source: In advanced malignancy, myeloid cells promote tumorigenesis by inhibiting CD8+ T cell mediated immune responses (Mitchem et al., 2013; Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2014), and myeloid cell depletion causes CD8+ T cell mediated epithelial cell death.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD8+ T cell depletion alone had no effect on PanIN progression in iKras* mice.
source: CD8+ T cell depletion alone had no effect on PanIN progression in iKras* mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Limited acinar cell recovery was induced by myeloid cell depletion and similarly observed when both CD8+ T cell and myeloid cells were depleted in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice.
source: Conversely, limited acinar cell recovery was induced by myeloid cell depletion (as described above) and similarly observed when both CD8+ T cell and myeloid cells were depleted in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: During the early stages of carcinogenesis, suppression of T cell-mediated immune responses does not appear to be the main function of infiltrating myeloid cells.
source: Thus, during the early stages of carcinogenesis, suppression of T cell-mediated immune responses does not appear to be the main function of infiltrating m cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing that CD8+ T cell depletion does not affect the outcome of myeloid cell depletion in early lesions.

claim: Abundant macrophages (CD11b+CD64+F4/80+) were detected in pancreata expressing oncogenic Kras as well as 3 days following Kras inactivation.
source: We detected abundant macrophages (CD11b+CD64+F4/80+) in pancreata expressing oncogenic Kras as well as 3 days following Kras inactivation, as determined by immunostaining and flow cytometry (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The total number of macrophages was significantly lower 1 week following Kras inactivation.
source: The total number of macrophages was significantly lower 1 week following Kras inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: In the presence of oncogenic Kras, most infiltrating macrophages were CD11b+CD64+F4/80+CD11c+CD206-, consistent with surface characteristics of tumor associated macrophages (TAMs).
source: In the presence of oncogenic Kras, most infiltrating macrophages were CD11b+CD64+F4/80+CD11c+CD206-, consistent with surface characteristics of tumor associated macrophages (TAMs) (Franklin et al., 2014;Noy and Pollard, 2014; Pollard, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: TAM infiltration decreased following Kras* inactivation, while CD11b+CD64+F4/80+CD206+CD11c- macrophages transiently increased.
source: TAM infiltration decreased following Kras* inactivation, while CD11b+CD64+F4/80+CD206+CD11c- macrophages transiently increased (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In myeloid cells extracted from oncogenic Kras expressing pancreata, elevated expression of Arginase 1 (Arg1) and Chitinase 3-like 3 (Chil3) was detected.
source: In myeloid cells extracted from oncogenic Kras expressing pancreata, we detected elevated expression of Arginase 1 (Arg1) and Chitinase 3-like 3 (Chil3) –also known as Ym1–mediators of the immune response and commonly expressed in TAMs (Geiger et al., 2016; Munder et al., 1998; Raes et al., 2002); both markers were downregulated in myeloid cells sorted following Kras inactivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Arg1 and Chil3 are mediators of the immune response and commonly expressed in TAMs.
source: In myeloid cells extracted from oncogenic Kras expressing pancreata, we detected elevated expression of Arginase 1 (Arg1) and Chitinase 3-like 3 (Chil3) –also known as Ym1–mediators of the immune response and commonly expressed in TAMs (Geiger et al., 2016; Munder et al., 1998; Raes et al., 2002); both markers were downregulated in myeloid cells sorted following Kras inactivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both Arg1 and Chil3 markers were downregulated in myeloid cells sorted following Kras inactivation.
source: In myeloid cells extracted from oncogenic Kras expressing pancreata, we detected elevated expression of Arginase 1 (Arg1) and Chitinase 3-like 3 (Chil3) –also known as Ym1–mediators of the immune response and commonly expressed in TAMs (Geiger et al., 2016; Munder et al., 1998; Raes et al., 2002); both markers were downregulated in myeloid cells sorted following Kras inactivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Macrophage polarization is regulated by the Kras status of epithelial cells.
source: Thus, macrophage polarization is regulated by the Kras status of epithelial cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing changes in macrophage markers upon Kras inactivation.

claim: Cancer cell conditioned media induced Arg1 expression in macrophages in an oncogenic Kras dependent manner.
source: Analysis of the RNA derived from the macrophages by qRT-PCR revealed that cancer cell conditioned media induced Arg1 expression in macrophages in an oncogenic Kras dependent manner (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Myeloid cells extracted from oncogenic Kras expressing pancreata revealed high levels of Hbegf, Tgfβ and Tumor necrosis factor-α (Tnfα).
source: Further characterization of myeloid cells extracted from oncogenic Kras expressing pancreata revealed high levels of Hbegf, Tgfβ and Tumor necrosis factor-α (Tnfα) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The expression of Hbegf, Tgfβ and Tnfα was reduced in myeloid cells isolated following Kras inactivation.
source: The expression of these ligands was reduced in myeloid cells isolated following Kras inactivation, while other secreted molecules, such as EGF and Tgfα, did not change (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3G.

claim: The expression of EGF and Tgfα in myeloid cells did not change following Kras inactivation.
source: The expression of these ligands was reduced in myeloid cells isolated following Kras inactivation, while other secreted molecules, such as EGF and Tgfα, did not change (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3G.

claim: Egfr expression was high when oncogenic Kras was expressed, and decreased upon its inactivation.
source: While Egfr expression was high when oncogenic Kras was expressed, and decreased upon its inactivation, Erbb4 was expressed at a lower level when Kras was active, but increased upon Kras inactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Erbb4 was expressed at a lower level when Kras was active, but increased upon Kras inactivation.
source: While Egfr expression was high when oncogenic Kras was expressed, and decreased upon its inactivation, Erbb4 was expressed at a lower level when Kras was active, but increased upon Kras inactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oncogenic Kras expression regulates the specific EGFR receptor expressed in the epithelium.
source: Thus, oncogenic Kras expression regulates the specific EGFR receptor expressed in the epithelium, as well as regulating polarization and expression of EGFR ligands in infiltrating myeloid cells through a non-cell autonomous mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing changes in EGFR receptor expression upon Kras inactivation.

claim: Oncogenic Kras expression regulates polarization and expression of EGFR ligands in infiltrating myeloid cells through a non-cell autonomous mechanism.
source: Thus, oncogenic Kras expression regulates the specific EGFR receptor expressed in the epithelium, as well as regulating polarization and expression of EGFR ligands in infiltrating myeloid cells through a non-cell autonomous mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing changes in myeloid cell behavior upon Kras inactivation in epithelial cells.

claim: During the early stages of carcinogenesis, oncogenic Kras, through activation of MAPK signaling, promotes dedifferentiation of acinar cells to ADM.
source: During the early stages of carcinogenesis, oncogenic Kras, through activation of MAPK signaling, promotes dedifferentiation of acinar cells to ADM (Collins et al., 2014; Halbrook et al., 2017; Houbracken et al., 2011; Strobel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acinar re-differentiation occurs upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras.
source: Conversely, acinar re-differentiation occurs upon inactivation of oncogenic Kras (Collins et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Intrinsic factors are known to regulate acinar redifferentiation.
source: While intrinsic factors are known to regulate acinar redifferentiation (Krah et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2013), the role of the microenvironment is less clear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The role of the microenvironment in acinar redifferentiation is less clear.
source: While intrinsic factors are known to regulate acinar redifferentiation (Krah et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2013), the role of the microenvironment is less clear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras during the early neoplastic stages leads to re-differentiation of acinar cells and remodeling of the extracellular matrix and fibro-inflammatory stroma.
source: In DT-treated iKras* mice, inactivation of oncogenic Kras during the early neoplastic stages leads to re-differentiation of acinar cells and remodeling of the extracellular matrix and fibro-inflammatory stroma (Figure 4B, Top Row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Depletion of myeloid cells severely impaired the re-differentiation of acinar cells and remodeling process following Kras inactivation.
source: In contrast, depletion of myeloid cells severely impaired this process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: A week after Kras inactivation, DT-treated iKras*;CD11b-DTR pancreata remained fibrotic with very few acinar units identified by histology.
source: A week after Kras inactivation, DT-treated iKras*;CD11b-DTR pancreata remained fibrotic with very few acinar units identified by histology (Figure 4B, Bottom Row, Trichrome staining in Figure 4C and pathological quantification in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and 4D.

claim: PAS staining, indicating mucinous ducts and low-grade PanINs, were still present in a subset of the ductal structures following myeloid cell depletion and Kras inactivation.
source: Furthermore, PAS staining, indicating mucinous ducts and low-grade PanINs, were still present in a subset of the ductal structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The epithelial cells in both iKras* and iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice after Kras* inactivation were derived from PanIN cells that had previously expressed the Kras* transgene.
source: Immunostaining for EGFP, a lineage tracing marker for Cre recombination, showed that the epithelial cells in both iKras* and iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice after Kras* inactivation were derived from PanIN cells that had previously expressed the Kras* transgene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon Kras inactivation, iKras* mice presented with a transient phase of co-expression of CK19 and amylase, prior to re-establishment of normal pancreas architecture.
source: Upon Kras inactivation, iKras* mice presented with a transient phase of co-expression of CK19 and amylase, prior to re-establishment of normal pancreas architecture (Figure 5A, Top Row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice, ductal structures with co-expression of CK19 and amylase persisted a week after Kras inactivation.
source: In contrast, in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice, ductal structures with co-expression of CK19 and amylase persisted a week after Kras inactivation (Figure 5A, Bottom Row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The newly recovered acinar cells in iKras* mice were highly proliferative.
source: The newly recovered acinar cells in iKras* mice were highly proliferative (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Proliferation was low in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice a week after Kras* inactivation.
source: In contrast, proliferation was low in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice a week after Kras* inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Apoptotic cells were rare in iKras* pancreata following Kras inactivation.
source: Conversely, apoptotic cells were rare in iKras* pancreata, but abundant in the epithelial compartment of iKras*;CD11b-DTR pancreata as shown by E-cadherin and cleaved caspase three co-immunostaining (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Apoptotic cells were abundant in the epithelial compartment of iKras*;CD11b-DTR pancreata following Kras inactivation.
source: Conversely, apoptotic cells were rare in iKras* pancreata, but abundant in the epithelial compartment of iKras*;CD11b-DTR pancreata as shown by E-cadherin and cleaved caspase three co-immunostaining (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CD8+ T cell depletion had no effects on either stroma remodeling or epithelial cell survival in iKras* mice following Kras inactivation.
source: In iKras* mice, CD8+ T cell depletion had no effects on either stroma remodeling or epithelial cell survival, and tissue remodeling occurred as expected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: CD8+ T cell depletion didn't improve cell survival in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice following Kras inactivation.
source: Interestingly, CD8+ T cell depletion didn't improve cell survival in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Acinar cell plasticity and survival was regulated by infiltrating myeloid cells, independently from their ability to regulate anti-tumor immune responses.
source: Thus, acinar cell plasticity and survival was regulated by infiltrating myeloid cells, independently from their ability to regulate anti-tumor immune responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing that CD8+ T cell depletion does not affect the outcome of myeloid cell depletion.

claim: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras in pre-neoplastic iKras* pancreata results in a reduction of epithelial p-ERK expression.
source: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras in pre-neoplastic iKras* pancreata results in a reduction of epithelial p-ERK expression (Collins et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: p-ERK downregulation in the epithelium coincided with a transient activation of p-ERK in the stroma following Kras inactivation.
source: Surprisingly, p-ERK downregulation in the epithelium coincided with a transient activation of p-ERK in the stroma (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: p-ERK was expressed in a subset of SMA+ cells following Kras inactivation.
source: SMA, a marker of activated fibroblasts, was rapidly reduced upon oncogenic Kras inactivation (Collins et al., 2012a); yet we observed expression of p-ERK in a subset of SMA+ cells (Figure 5C, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Extensive co-localization of p-ERK with the fibroblast markers Vimentin and Platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ) was observed following Kras inactivation.
source: We observed extensive co-localization of p-ERK with the fibroblast markers Vimentin and Platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: F4/80+ macrophages only rarely expressed measurable but low levels of p-ERK following Kras inactivation.
source: In contrast, F4/80+ macrophages only rarely expressed measurable but low levels of p-ERK (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Myeloid cell ablation prevented p-ERK up-regulation in the stroma upon Kras inactivation.
source: Interestingly, myeloid cell ablation prevented p-ERK up-regulation in the stroma upon Kras inactivation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Myeloid cells provide essential factors that activate EGFR/MAPK signaling in stromal fibroblasts.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that myeloid cells provide essential factors that activate EGFR/MAPK signaling in stromal fibroblasts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing that myeloid cell depletion prevents p-ERK activation in fibroblasts.

claim: Egf and Tgfα levels were significantly up-regulated in iKras* pancreata 3 days following Kras* inactivation.
source: Egf and Tgfα levels were significantly up-regulated in iKras* pancreata 3 days following Kras* inactivation, whereas the levels of other EGFR ligands Hbegf, Areg and Ereg were high in neoplastic pancreata (Kras* ON) and dramatically down-regulated when Kras* was inactivated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The levels of EGFR ligands Hbegf, Areg and Ereg were high in neoplastic pancreata (Kras* ON) and dramatically down-regulated when Kras* was inactivated.
source: Egf and Tgfα levels were significantly up-regulated in iKras* pancreata 3 days following Kras* inactivation, whereas the levels of other EGFR ligands Hbegf, Areg and Ereg were high in neoplastic pancreata (Kras* ON) and dramatically down-regulated when Kras* was inactivated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Depletion of myeloid cells prevented the increase in Egf and Tgfα upon Kras inactivation.
source: Depletion of myeloid cells prevented the increase in Egf and Tgfα upon Kras inactivation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mmp1 was upregulated in iKras* pancreata 3 days following Kras* inactivation.
source: Among the MMPs we examined, Mmp1 was upregulated in iKras* pancreata 3 days following Kras* inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: A similar trend for Mmp2 and Mmp9 upregulation was observed following Kras inactivation, while the expression of Mmp12 and Mmp14 did not change.
source: We observed a similar trend for Mmp2 and Mmp9 while the expression of Mmp12 and Mmp14 did not change.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: MMP expression was slightly (but not significantly) decreased upon myeloid cell depletion following Kras inactivation.
source: However, their expression was slightly (but not significantly) decreased upon myeloid cell depletion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Egf and Tgfα were present in both myeloid cells and fibroblasts, at similar levels independently from the oncogenic Kras status.
source: qRT-PCR analysis showed that Egf and Tgfα were present in both myeloid cells and fibroblasts, at similar levels independently from the oncogenic Kras status (Figure 3G and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 6B.

claim: Hbegf was expressed in a Kras-dependent manner in myeloid cells, but not expressed in fibroblasts.
source: Hbegf, as mentioned earlier, was expressed in a Kras-dependent manner in myeloid cells (Figure 3G), but not expressed in fibroblasts (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and stated observation.

claim: EGFR was expressed in fibroblasts independently of epithelial Kras status.
source: EGFR was expressed in fibroblasts independently of epithelial Kras status (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The EGFR/MAPK pathway regulates expression of ECM degrading enzymes in various types of cells including fibroblasts.
source: The EGFR/MAPK pathway regulates expression of ECM degrading enzymes in various types of cells including fibroblasts (Kajanne et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MMPs expression was detected in both myeloid cells and fibroblasts.
source: Accordingly, MMPs expression was detected in both myeloid cells and fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Mmp2 expression in fibroblasts derived from iKras* was up-regulated when Kras* was OFF for 3 days and significantly higher compared to that in fibroblasts derived from iKras*;CD11b-DTR.
source: In particular, Mmp2 expression in fibroblasts derived from iKras* was up-regulated when Kras* was OFF for 3 days and significantly higher compared to that in fibroblasts derived from iKras*;CD11b-DTR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Mmp9 expression in fibroblasts decreased upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: Further, Mmp9 expression in fibroblasts decreased upon myeloid cell depletion (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Western-blot analysis of the pancreata showed a reduction in overall Mmp2 protein levels, and specifically the active form of the protein, upon myeloid cell depletion.
source: Western-blot analysis of the pancreata showed a reduction in overall Mmp2 protein levels, and specifically the active form of the protein, upon myeloid cell depletion (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Western-blot analysis revealed a decrease in Collagen I levels following Kras* inactivation in iKras* mice but not in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice, indicating impaired remodeling in the latter.
source: Interestingly, Western-blot analysis also revealed a decrease in Collagen I levels following Kras* inactivation in iKras* mice but not in iKras*;CD11b-DTR mice, indicating impaired remodeling in the latter (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Epithelial cells might constitute a source of EGFR ligands.
source: In addition to myeloid cells, epithelial cells might constitute a source of EGFR ligands.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Expression of Egf, Tgfα and Hbegf mRNA was detected in sorted epithelial cells.
source: By q-PCR analysis, we detected expression of Egf, Tgfα and Hbegf mRNA in sorted epithelial cells; the expression of Egf was decreased upon myeloid cell depletion while expression of the other ligands was unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of Egf in epithelial cells was decreased upon myeloid cell depletion while expression of Tgfα and Hbegf was unchanged.
source: By q-PCR analysis, we detected expression of Egf, Tgfα and Hbegf mRNA in sorted epithelial cells; the expression of Egf was decreased upon myeloid cell depletion while expression of the other ligands was unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myeloid cells might contribute to EGFR ligand levels both by expressing them directly, and by inducing their expression in other cells types.
source: Based on our data, myeloid cells might contribute to EGFR ligand levels both by expressing them directly, and by inducing their expression in other cells types (epithelial, and possibly others).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing EGFR ligand expression in multiple cell types.

claim: EGFR inhibition (EGFRi) blocked MAPK activation in the stroma following Kras inactivation.
source: EGFR inhibition (EGFRi) blocked MAPK activation in the stroma as measured by reduced p-ERK levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: EGFRi treatment resulted in delayed tissue repair, with abundant stroma still present at 1 week post Kras* inactivation.
source: Similar to myeloid cell depletion, EGFRi treatment resulted in delayed tissue repair. Abundant stroma was still present at 1 week post Kras* inactivation (Figure 7B, HE and Trichrome staining).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mmp2 and Mmp9 expression was inhibited in EGFRi treated pancreata 3–7 days post Kras* inactivation.
source: Further, Mmp2 and Mmp9 expression was inhibited in EGFRi treated pancreata 3–7 days post Kras* inactivation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Acinar re-differentiation was not affected by EGFRi treatment.
source: However, acinar re-differentiation was not affected by EGFRi treatment, as shown by co-immunofluorescent staining for CK19 and amylase (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MEK inhibition (MEKi) upon Kras* inactivation resulted in reduced ECM degradation and MMPs expression.
source: We made similar observations upon MEK inhibition (MEKi) upon Kras* inactivation, with reduced ECM degradation and MMPs expression (Figure 8B and C), but unimpaired acinar re-differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: MEKi treatment did not impair acinar re-differentiation following Kras inactivation.
source: We made similar observations upon MEK inhibition (MEKi) upon Kras* inactivation, with reduced ECM degradation and MMPs expression (Figure 8B and C), but unimpaired acinar re-differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: EGFR-MAPK signaling is required for ECM degradation and remodeling.
source: Therefore, EGFR-MAPK signaling is required for ECM degradation and remodeling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing that EGFR and MEK inhibition impair ECM remodeling.

claim: In the epithelium, repression of EGFR/MAPK promoted re-differentiation.
source: Conversely, in the epithelium, repression of EGFR/MAPK promoted re-differentiation, consistent with previous studies (Ardito et al., 2012; Collins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The pancreas has a limited ability to regenerate following injury in the adult.
source: The pancreas is formed by a limited number of progenitor cells and, in the adult, it has a limited ability to regenerate following injury (Dor et al., 2004), although it can grow in response to increase need for its exocrine or endocrine function (Holtz et al., 2014; Karnik et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The pancreas can grow in response to increase need for its exocrine or endocrine function.
source: The pancreas is formed by a limited number of progenitor cells and, in the adult, it has a limited ability to regenerate following injury (Dor et al., 2004), although it can grow in response to increase need for its exocrine or endocrine function (Holtz et al., 2014; Karnik et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The pancreas is highly plastic.
source: The pancreas is highly plastic; in particular, acinar cells can de-differentiate into duct-like cells during a process known as acinar-ductal metaplasia (ADM).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: ADM leads to a cell type that is susceptible to transformation by oncogenic Kras.
source: While ADM is important during tissue damage such as acute pancreatitis -where it might protect acinar cells from further damage and set the stage for repair- it also leads to a cell type that is susceptible to transformation by oncogenic Kras (for review see [Morris et al., 2010; Roy and Hebrok, 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: ADM is characterized by loss of acinar differentiation and acquisition of a duct-like phenotype which is accompanied by expression of pancreas progenitor markers.
source: ADM is characterized by loss of acinar differentiation and acquisition of a duct-like phenotype which is accompanied by expression of pancreas progenitor markers (Puri and Hebrok, 2010; Roy and Hebrok, 2015; Stanger and Hebrok, 2013; Storz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcription factors driving acinar differentiation are down-regulated during ADM.
source: Transcription factors driving acinar differentiation are down-regulated during ADM.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: BHLHA15 expression is lost during ADM and re-established when ADM re-differentiates to acini.
source: BHLHA15 expression is lost during ADM and re-established when ADM re-differentiates to acini.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: BHLHA15 plays a functional role in acinar differentiation, and while BHLHA15 loss facilitates ADM (and, consequently, carcinogenesis), forced expression of BHLHA15 is protective against both ADM and carcinogenesis.
source: Importantly, BHLHA15 plays a functional role in this process, and while BHLHA15 loss facilitates ADM (and, consequently, carcinogenesis), forced expression of BHLHA15 is protective against both ADM and carcinogenesis (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ptf1a is expressed throughout the pancreatic bud early in development, but it is restricted to acinar cells in the adult organ.
source: The transcription factor Ptf1a is expressed throughout the pancreatic bud early in development, but it is restricted to acinar cells in the adult organ (Kawaguchi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ptf1a loss facilitates ADM and carcinogenesis.
source: Ptf1a loss facilitates ADM and carcinogenesis (Krah et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PDX1, a key determinant of pancreas development expressed at low levels in adult acini, is important to maintain acinar cell identity.
source: Further, PDX1, a key determinant of pancreas development expressed at low levels in adult acini, is similarly important to maintain acinar cell identity (Roy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Signals intrinsic to epithelial cells regulate the differentiation status of acinar cells.
source: Thus, signals intrinsic to epithelial cells regulate the differentiation status of acinar cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the previous statements about transcription factors.

claim: Oncogenic Kras induces ADM through activation of MAPK signaling.
source: We have, and others, have previously shown that oncogenic Kras induces ADM through activation of MAPK signaling (Ardito et al., 2012; Collins et al., 2014; Collisson et al., 2012) and consequent repression of acinar-specific transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oncogenic Kras induces ADM through consequent repression of acinar-specific transcription factors.
source: We have, and others, have previously shown that oncogenic Kras induces ADM through activation of MAPK signaling (Ardito et al., 2012; Collins et al., 2014; Collisson et al., 2012) and consequent repression of acinar-specific transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of MAPK signaling using MEK inhibitors allows re-expression of acinar-specific transcription factors and re-differentiation of acinar cells.
source: Conversely, inhibition of MAPK signaling using MEK inhibitors allows re-expression of acinar-specific transcription factors and re-differentiation of acinar cells (Collins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: A complex network of intrinsic signals regulates acinar differentiation in the adult pancreas.
source: Thus, a complex network of intrinsic signals regulates acinar differentiation in the adult pancreas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the previous statements about transcription factors and signaling pathways.

claim: Myeloid cells play an instructive role regulating epithelial cell identity and plasticity.
source: In this study, we show that myeloid cells play an instructive role regulating epithelial cell identity and plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: In the presence of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells are required to maintain dedifferentiation of ADM/low-grade PanIN lesions.
source: In the presence of oncogenic Kras, myeloid cells are required to maintain dedifferentiation of ADM/low-grade PanIN lesions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Depletion of myeloid cells induces BHLHA15 expression and occasionally expression of the digestive enzyme amylase in low-grade PanINs, notwithstanding expression of oncogenic Kras.
source: Depletion of myeloid cells induces BHLHA15 expression and occasionally expression of the digestive enzyme amylase in low-grade PanINs, notwithstanding expression of oncogenic Kras, thus presumably preventing further progression to malignancy.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion presumably prevents further progression to malignancy.
source: Depletion of myeloid cells induces BHLHA15 expression and occasionally expression of the digestive enzyme amylase in low-grade PanINs, notwithstanding expression of oncogenic Kras, thus presumably preventing further progression to malignancy.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that myeloid cell depletion induces acinar differentiation markers.

claim: Myeloid cells are required for the expression of EGF ligands, and activation of MAPK signaling in pancreatic epithelial cells.
source: We show that myeloid cells are required for the expression of EGF ligands, and activation of MAPK signaling in pancreatic epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Oncogenic Kras is insufficient to induce a high enough level of MAPK activation to induce transformation.
source: This finding fits with the notion that oncogenic Kras is insufficient to induce a high enough level of MAPK activation to induce transformation (Daniluk et al., 2012), thus EGFR ligands are required for carcinogenesis (Ardito et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EGFR ligands are required for carcinogenesis.
source: This finding fits with the notion that oncogenic Kras is insufficient to induce a high enough level of MAPK activation to induce transformation (Daniluk et al., 2012), thus EGFR ligands are required for carcinogenesis (Ardito et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In tumor-bearing mice, myeloid cells inhibit CD8+ T cell mediated anti-tumor immune responses, and this function explains their requirement in cancer growth.
source: In tumor-bearing mice, myeloid cells inhibit CD8+ T cell mediated anti-tumor immune responses, and this function explains their requirement in cancer growth (Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both during the progression of early PanIN lesions and during their regression upon Kras inactivation, myeloid cell-requirement was independent from the presence of CD8+ T cells.
source: However, both during the progression of early PanIN lesions and during their regression upon Kras inactivation, myeloid cell-requirement was independent from the presence of CD8+ T cells, indicating that they play a function distinct from immune suppression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Upon Kras inactivation, myeloid cells including re-polarized M2 macrophages are required for tissue remodeling.
source: Upon Kras inactivation, myeloid cells including re-polarized M2 macrophages are required for tissue remodeling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Myeloid cells are required for epithelial cell re-differentiation and survival following Kras inactivation.
source: First, we show that myeloid cells are required for epithelial cell re-differentiation and survival.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion results in epithelial cell death and persistence of clusters of cells co-expressing acinar and ductal markers following Kras inactivation.
source: Thus, myeloid cell depletion results in epithelial cell death and persistence of clusters of cells co-expressing acinar and ductal markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Myeloid cells are required for remodeling of the extracellular matrix following Kras inactivation.
source: Second, we show that myeloid cells are required for remodeling of the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Myeloid cells are required to sustain activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in epithelial cells.
source: We have previously shown that myeloid cells are required to sustain activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in epithelial cells (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: MAPK signaling is necessary for PanIN formation and progression.
source: In turn, MAPK signaling is necessary for PanIN formation and progression (Ardito et al., 2012; Collins et al., 2014; Collisson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Remodeling of the extracellular matrix was regulated by EGFR/MAPK signaling.
source: Surprisingly, remodeling of the extracellular matrix was also regulated by EGFR/MAPK signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras in the pancreas led to changes of expression of specific EGFR ligands in the pancreas.
source: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras in the pancreas led to changes of expression of specific EGFR ligands in the pancreas.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: In presence of active Kras, Hbegf, Areg and Ereg were the main EGFR ligands.
source: In presence of active Kras, Hbegf, Areg and Ereg were the main ligands.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Upon Kras* inactivation, the expression of Hbegf, Areg and Ereg decreased while that of Egf and Tgfα increased.
source: Upon Kras* inactivation, their expression decreased while that of Egf and Tgfα increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Inactivation of oncogenic Kras resulted in transient activation of MAPK signaling in stromal fibroblasts, simultaneous to loss of activation in the epithelium.
source: Remarkably, inactivation of oncogenic Kras resulted in transient activation of MAPK signaling in stromal fibroblasts, simultaneous to loss of activation in the epithelium.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Treatment with Erlotinib (EGFR inhibitor) or Tramatinib (MEK inhibitor) resulted in the persistence of pancreatic fibrosis following Kras inactivation.
source: Consistent with the notion that MAPK signaling in the stroma is important for remodeling, treatment with Erlotinib (EGFR inhibitor) or Tramatinib (MEK inhibitor) resulted in the persistence of pancreatic fibrosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in different cellular compartments might, in turn, favor carcinogenesis or remodeling.
source: The observation that activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in different cellular compartments might, in turn, favor carcinogenesis or remodeling has potential clinical implications, suggesting that specific inhibition of distinct EGFR ligands or receptors might be preferable to overall inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data with speculation about clinical implications.

claim: Specific inhibition of distinct EGFR ligands or receptors might be preferable to overall inhibition.
source: The observation that activation of EGFR/MAPK signaling in different cellular compartments might, in turn, favor carcinogenesis or remodeling has potential clinical implications, suggesting that specific inhibition of distinct EGFR ligands or receptors might be preferable to overall inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: Myeloid cells are a source of EGFR ligands.
source: While our data support the notion that myeloid cells are a source of EGFR ligands, they also support the idea that myeloid cells induce EGFR ligands in other cellular compartments, including epithelial cells; future studies will need to address the role of specific EGFR ligands and their specific cell sources.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing EGFR ligand expression in myeloid cells.

claim: Myeloid cells induce EGFR ligands in other cellular compartments, including epithelial cells.
source: While our data support the notion that myeloid cells are a source of EGFR ligands, they also support the idea that myeloid cells induce EGFR ligands in other cellular compartments, including epithelial cells; future studies will need to address the role of specific EGFR ligands and their specific cell sources.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in EGFR ligand expression in epithelial cells upon myeloid cell depletion.

claim: The cross-talk between epithelial cells and myeloid cells regulates pancreatic plasticity and fibrosis.
source: In summary, in this study we show that the cross-talk between epithelial cells and myeloid cells regulates pancreatic plasticity and fibrosis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The cross-talk between epithelial cells and myeloid cells is important for pancreatic tissue repair following injury.
source: Further, we show that this cross-talk is important for pancreatic tissue repair following injury, but can be co-opted, in presence of oncogenic Kras, to promote carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The cross-talk between epithelial cells and myeloid cells can be co-opted, in presence of oncogenic Kras, to promote carcinogenesis.
source: Further, we show that this cross-talk is important for pancreatic tissue repair following injury, but can be co-opted, in presence of oncogenic Kras, to promote carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Manipulating the cross-talk between epithelial cells and myeloid cells to promote repair while inhibiting carcinogenesis should be prioritized in future studies.
source: Manipulating this cross-talk to promote repair while inhibiting carcinogenesis should therefore be prioritized in future studies.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings of the study.
